title: Whose is it, and the extended family
goal: Show possession with کا / کے / کی and name family members — including six words for relatives that English lumps together as "uncle", "aunt", "grandfather", and "grandmother".
bekal: use کا، کے، کی to match the thing owned
use the possessives میرا، تمہارا، آپ کا، اس کا، ہمارا، ان کا

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — خاندان کی تصویر
dialogs.intro: Still in the living room. Budi stands in front of the family photo and starts asking about everyone, one by one.

notes: **The possessive follows the thing owned, not the owner.** The phrase آپ کے والد کی تصویر means "your father's photo", and it contains two possessive markers. The first, کے, appears because والد is followed by another postposition; the second, کی, appears because **تصویر is feminine**. Not because the father is male. This is the one learners get backwards most often.

**Urdu has no single word for "older" or "younger" sibling.** The word بھائی means brother, full stop — just like English. If age matters, add an adjective: بڑا بھائی (older brother), چھوٹی بہن (younger sister). Literally "big brother" and "little sister", exactly as in English.

**On the other hand, Urdu is far more precise about uncles and aunts.** English has one "uncle" and one "aunt"; Urdu has four words, and you **must** pick the right one. چچا = **father's** brother. ماموں = **mother's** brother. پھوپھی = **father's** sister. خالہ = **mother's** sister. Picking the wrong one doesn't sound like a slip of the tongue — it sounds like you've got the family tree wrong.

**Grandparents split along two lines too.** The words دادا and دادی are grandfather and grandmother on your **father's side**; نانا and نانی on your **mother's side**. If you tell a Pakistani about your grandfather, they'll know instantly from the word you choose which one you mean — and they really do want to know.

**The phrase ماشاءاللہ is used far more widely than you might think.** It isn't just a religious expression but **a way of praising something without sounding envious**. A clever child, a lovely house, any good news — ماشاءاللہ. Its cousins: انشاءاللہ (for plans that haven't happened yet), الحمد للہ (in reply to "how are you?"), جزاک اللہ (a deeper thank-you).

**The words خاتون and صاحب are everyday courtesy.** خاتون (*ḵātūn*) = "lady, madam", the polite way to refer to a woman you don't know. صاحب (*sāhab*) goes after a man's name: علی صاحب and ڈاکٹر صاحب. For women there's صاحبہ, or more commonly باجی (big sister) in casual speech.

grammars.title: کا، کے، کی — one marker, three faces
body: Urdu has no possessive ending like English *'s* on the owner. Instead it uses a little word that stands **between the owner and the thing owned**, and its form is chosen by **the thing owned**.
The pattern: **owner + کا/کے/کی + thing**. علی کا گھر = "Ali's house", literally "Ali of house".

head: Form
Used when the thing owned is
Example
Meaning
rows: علی کی کتاب · علی کی کتابیں
masculine plural, or before another postposition
علی کے بیٹے · علی کے گھر میں

after: Pronouns have their own ready-made forms, and these are the ones you'll say most: **میرا/میری/میرے** (my), **تمہارا/تمہاری/تمہارے** (your, familiar), **آپ کا/کی/کے** (your, polite), **اس کا/کی/کے** (his/her), **ہمارا/ہماری/ہمارے** (our), **ان کا/کی/کے** (their).

⚠️ Notice that three forms — میرا · تمہارا · ہمارا — stand alone without کا, because they already contain it. Writing میرا کا is a mistake. On the other hand آپ and اس and ان still need کا, so the forms are آپ کا نام · اس کی بہن · ان کے بھائی.

grammars.title: Saying "have" for relatives
body: Urdu has three different ways of saying "have", and the choice depends on **what is had**. Unit 17 sorts out all three. Today you only need one: for **relatives**, use the ordinary possessive plus ہے/ہیں.

head: Urdu sentence
Say it
Literally
rows: my one brother is — *I have one brother*
my two sisters are — *I have two sisters*
you of how-many children are — *how many children do you have?*
ان کا کوئی بھائی نہیں ہے۔
un kā koī bhāī nahīñ hai.
them of any brother not is — *he has no brothers*

after: ⚠️ This pattern is **only** for relatives and body parts. For things you can move around — money, books, a car, time — use کے پاس, as in میرے پاس پیسے ہیں ("I have money"). Saying میرا پیسہ ہے for "I have money" isn't ungrammatical, but it means "that money is mine". Unit 17 deals with this.

head: Urdu
Say it
Meaning
Note
rows: ابو is more intimate — what children call their dad
also an affectionate way to address any young person

blocks.title: Asking about family is friendly, not nosy
items: In Pakistan, the question آپ کے کتنے بھائی بہن ہیں؟ ("how many brothers and sisters do you have?") is a normal way to open a conversation with someone you've just met — like "what do you do?" in the West. A short answer actually sounds cold.
The question آپ شادی شدہ ہیں؟ ("are you married?") is also much more ordinary than in the West, and it isn't meant to pry. A safe answer: جی ہاں or جی نہیں، ابھی نہیں ("not yet").
If you'd like to close the topic politely without answering, use the line Pakistanis use themselves: الحمد للہ، سب ٹھیک ہے ("thank God, all is well") — and the conversation moves on by itself.
